title: U.S. Open recorded $640 million revenues for 2025, with impact of luxury renovation still to come
content:
The 2025 U.S. Open further established it as the most lucrative event in tennis, and one of the most lucrative annual events in sports.

It recorded nearly $640 million in revenue last year, which accounted for 90 percent of the U.S. Tennis Association’s annual revenue of over $708 million, according to the organization’s audited financial statements. Operating expenses for the tournament came in at $324 million, The figures put the 2026 edition on track to clear $700 million in revenue, following a steep rise in prices for the tournament’s most sought-after and expensive tickets during an $800 million renovation of Arthur Ashe Stadium, the tournament’s largest.

The figures mean that player prize money of $90 million accounted for 14 percent of revenue, the calculation that the group of top-10 men’s and women’s players pushing for better compensation uses to benchmark its efforts. In 2025, $100 million sales of corporate hospitality and services at the U.S. Open, with a marginal contribution from other events, paid for that prize money with $10 million left over.

The U.S. Open set attendance records in 2025, with 1.1 million fans coming through during the three-week event, which included the qualifying tournament and the mixed doubles competition. It set another record of over 1.2 million in 2026. Wimbledon, its closest competitor among the Grand Slams, has 14 days of main-draw play compared to 15 and does not have a week of on-site buildup. It also does not sell separate tickets for day and night sessions, with an 11 p.m. curfew. It recorded revenues of $566 million in 2025.

The report on the financial success of the U.S. Open comes at the end of a year of turmoil for tennis relating to player pay and conditions. A small group of active and retired players and the Professional Tennis Players Association have seen motions to dismiss their antitrust lawsuit against the Grand Slams and tours rejected this fall. The operators of the French Open, Wimbledon and the U.S. Open are still defending the lawsuit, alongside the ATP and WTA. Tennis Australia settled with the PTPA last year.

At the same time, the top-10 player group intensified its efforts over compensation, staging brief media protests at the French Open and Wimbledon. In response, the U.S. Open offered prize money of $108 million for this year’s edition, and joined with the other Grand Slams in agreeing to the creation of a player council, which will negotiate prize money with each organization separately.

The group is seeking 22 percent of revenue in prize money from each Grand Slam by 2030, but the organizers of all four are on record as saying that they do not believe revenue is the right metric to measure compensation against.

The USTA is a non-profit and invests in its mission to grow the sport in the United States. The organization spent nearly $300 million in 2025 on everything from recreational play, to construction of new facilities, coaching, and holding tournaments and running its foundation.

Still, it came under fire this summer as ticket prices sky-rocketed. The most startling increases were on the official resale market, which the USTA does not control, though it could negotiate a resale agreement with operator Ticketmaster. But they came in conjunction with the first part of the renovation of Arthur Ashe Stadium, which increased the proportion of the most expensive seats in the bowl and will have added nine hospitality clubs once it is completed.

The financial windfall from the first part of the renovation won’t become clear for another year, since public reporting of revenues is a year behind. But it is on track to be done before the 2027 edition, and will again transform the experience of the event — as well as the USTA’s balance sheets.
